transcript.text: Potter. Tell us about a time during an operation — not the war, we've all read those books — an ordinary operation when you failed, and it was entirely your fault, and someone got hurt because of it. How did you handle it?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
I... It's not something I'm particularly proud of, but I do remember a mission about two years ago. We were tracking a group of Death Eaters who had taken over a small town in the Midlands. The operation was straightforward: gather intelligence, locate the nest, extract the Dark巫师, and clean up the area. We had it all planned out.

But I... I was too eager. I wanted to prove myself, to show that I was ready for bigger missions. I pushed us to move in too quickly, without waiting for the full Intel to come in. We walked into an ambush, and... and it was a mess. One of our newer agents, a wizard named PC Crouch, was gravely injured. He's still in St. Mungo's, and may never be able to return to field work.

I... I took it hard. I felt responsible, and I should have been. I let my own ambitions cloud my judgment, and it cost us all. I spent a lot of time with PC, trying to help him with his recovery, and made it a point to spend more time with his family, to try and ease the burden.

But the most important thing... I changed my approach. I became more patient, more willing to listen and learn from others' experience. I still have a fire in me, but now it's a controlled burn, not a blaze that can get out of hand. I've worked hard to be a better team player, to rely on the expertise of my colleagues, and to trust the process, even when it feels slow.

I know I'll never be able to make up for what happened to PC, but I've tried to honor his service by becoming the best Auror I can be. And that's... that's something I'll continue to do, every day.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text: It takes a lot to own up to a mistake like that, Potter. It's one thing to make a misstep, but it's another to learn from it and make sure it doesn't happen again. How do you plan on incorporating these lessons into your training with new recruits? What would you tell them to prevent something similar from happening in the future?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
I'd tell them that... that confidence is great, but it can be a double-edged sword. I'd stress the importance of listening, of really hearing what your team is saying. It's not just about following orders; it's about understanding the rationale behind them.

I'd encourage them to ask questions, to seek out the perspectives of more experienced Aurors. And not just in a formal setting, either. I'd tell them to take advantage of the informal interactions, the casual conversations that can happen over a cup of tea or at the pub. Those are often where you pick up the most valuable insights.

I'd also make sure they understand that it's okay to have a strong sense of mission, to want to be out there, making a difference. But that passion has to be balanced with... with a sense of responsibility. It's about knowing when to push and when to pull back. It's about recognizing when you're in over your head and being humble enough to ask for help.

And finally, I'd tell them that every operation, no matter how routine it seems, is an opportunity to learn. I'd urge them to approach each mission with an open mind, to be ready to adapt and to trust their instincts, but also to trust their team.

I... I know I'm still learning, too. None of us are perfect, but we can all strive to be better. And if we can pass that ethos on to the next generation of Aurors, then maybe... maybe we can prevent mistakes like the one I made from happening again.
